lead: The Clausius–Clapeyron equation gives the slope of a saturation curve from latent heat and volume change. It answers a practical question: water boils at 373 K at 1 atm, so what is its vapour pressure at 350 K? One measured (P, T) pair plus ΔH gives another. A plot of ln P against 1/T gives ΔH. Chemical engineers use it for steam, refrigerants, distillation and vacuum drying.
prereq: You need two-phase properties from property tables and diagrams, the equality of Gibbs energy at equilibrium from Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies, and phase diagrams and latent heat from the PVT-behaviour chapters.

blocks.text: At saturation, liquid and vapour coexist. The saturation curve P<sub>sat</sub>(T) has a slope. Equality of Gibbs free energy of the two phases gives the Clapeyron equation:

blocks.where: P<sub>sat</sub> is saturation pressure (Pa), T is absolute temperature (K), ΔH is latent heat (J/mol), and ΔV = V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub> is molar volume change (m³/mol).

blocks.text: Derivation: along the coexistence curve G<sub>l</sub> = G<sub>g</sub>, so a small step keeps dG<sub>l</sub> = dG<sub>g</sub>: −S<sub>l</sub> dT + V<sub>l</sub> dP = −S<sub>g</sub> dT + V<sub>g</sub> dP. Rearranging, dP/dT = (S<sub>g</sub> − S<sub>l</sub>)/(V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub>) = ΔS/ΔV, and at equilibrium ΔS = ΔH/T.

A large ΔH makes the curve steep. A large ΔV makes it flatter. For vaporisation ΔV > 0, so dPsat/dT > 0. For ice melting, ΔV = Vliquid − Vsolid < 0, so dPsat/dT < 0: the melting point falls as pressure rises, but only slightly, by about 0.0074 K per bar (worked example 2). The same equation also follows from the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)T = (∂P/∂T)V of Maxwell relations applied across the two-phase region, where ∂S/∂V = ΔS/ΔV = ΔH/(TΔV). The equation is exact for a pure substance at coexistence; no ideal-gas assumption is used yet. ΔH is the enthalpy change from phase 1 to phase 2; its sign follows the direction. For vaporisation, ΔH is positive and the pressure rises with temperature. It is the starting point for the ideal-vapour form below.

sections.h3: Ideal-vapour form and the straight line

blocks.text: For liquid–vapour saturation away from the critical point, V<sub>g</sub> ≫ V<sub>l</sub>, so ΔV ≈ V<sub>g</sub>. Treat the vapour as ideal: V<sub>g</sub> = RT/P<sub>sat</sub>, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Substitution gives:

blocks.where: P<sub>sat</sub> is saturation pressure, T is absolute temperature, ΔH is molar latent heat, and R is the gas constant.

blocks.text: Integrate from (P1, T1) to (P2, T2). For constant ΔH:

blocks.where: P1 and P2 are saturation pressures in the same unit, T1 and T2 are in K, ΔH is in J/mol, and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

blocks.text: Equivalently, ln P<sub>sat</sub> = A − ΔH/(R T). A plot of ln P<sub>sat</sub> against 1/T is a straight line with slope −ΔH/R. Two measured points give ΔH = −R ln(P2/P1)/(1/T2 − 1/T1). To estimate P2, use P2 = P1 exp[−(ΔH/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1)]. Convert T to kelvin and keep pressures in one unit. The figure shows water with ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.65 kJ/mol. Accuracy: the true vapour pressure of water at 350 K is 41.7 kPa, so the estimate of worked example 1 (42.8 kPa) is 2.7 % high, mainly because ΔH<sub>vap</sub> grows as the temperature falls.

figure.caption: The Clausius–Clapeyron line for water, ln P against 1/T with slope −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R = −4889 K, drawn through the normal boiling point. Dots are steam-table pressures from 330 K to 373 K; the line predicts 42.8 kPa at 350 K against the true 41.7 kPa, because ΔH<sub>vap</sub> grows as the temperature falls.

examples.question: Water has ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.65 kJ/mol and a normal boiling point of 373 K at 1 atm (101.325 kPa). Estimate its saturation pressure at 350 K using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
examples.answer: The estimated saturation pressure of water at 350 K is 42.8 kPa, about 0.428 bar.
examples.check:
import math
dH = 40650.0
R = 8.314
T1 = 373.0
T2 = 350.0
P1 = 101.325
ln_ratio = -(dH / R) * (1/T2 - 1/T1)
P2 = P1 * math.exp(ln_ratio)
print(round(ln_ratio, 4))
print(round(P2, 1))
print(round(P2 / 100, 3))

examples.question: Ice melts at 273.15 K with ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 6.01 kJ/mol. The molar volumes are 19.65 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol for ice and 18.02 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol for water. Find the slope of the melting curve, the pressure needed to lower the melting point by 1 K, and the effect of a 70 bar skate blade.
steps: ΔV = V<sub>l</sub> − V<sub>s</sub> = 18.02 × 10⁻⁶ − 19.65 × 10⁻⁶ = −1.63 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol: water is denser than ice.
To lower the melting point by 1 K needs about 135 bar; the reciprocal slope is dT/dP = −1/135.0 = −0.0074 K/bar.
A 70 kg skater (weight 687 N, call it 700 N) on 1 cm² of blade presses with 700/(1 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.0 × 10⁶ Pa = 70 bar.
Melting-point drop: 70/135.0 = 0.52 K. So at −10 °C the ice under the blade stays solid; pressure melting cannot explain skating.
The ideal-vapour form cannot be used here: both phases are condensed, so ΔV is small and no gas law applies.
examples.answer: dP/dT = −135.0 bar/K; about 135 bar per kelvin of lowering; a 70 bar blade lowers the melting point by only 0.52 K.
examples.check:
H = 6010.0
T = 273.15
dV = 18.02e-6 - 19.65e-6
slope = H / (T * dV) / 1e5
print(round(slope, 1), round(70 / -slope, 2))

traps: Using T in °C. The equation needs kelvin; a Celsius value makes 1/T and ΔH/R(1/T2 − 1/T1) the wrong size, so the estimated pressure is badly wrong.
Dropping the minus sign in ln(P2/P1) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1).
Using V<sub>l</sub> instead of ΔV = V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub>; for vaporisation the gas volume dominates.
Mixing pressure units in P2/P1; the ratio is dimensionless, so P1 and P2 must match.
Taking the slope from P against T; −ΔH/R is the slope of ln P against 1/T.

Believing that ice skating works by pressure melting. Even 70 bar under a skate lowers the melting point by only about 0.5 K; skating at −10 °C works because of friction heating and a thin liquid-like surface layer.

quiz.q: State the Clapeyron equation and define ΔV.
Why is ΔV ≈ V<sub>g</sub> valid for liquid–vapour saturation?
quiz.a: V<sub>g</sub> is much larger than V<sub>l</sub> away from the critical point.

quiz.q: Water: ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.65 kJ/mol, T1 = 373 K, P1 = 101.3 kPa. Estimate P<sub>sat</sub> at 360 K.
A plot of ln P<sub>sat</sub> against 1/T has slope −3200 K. Find ΔH<sub>vap</sub>.
Write the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation for constant ΔH.
Why does the ideal-vapour form fail near the critical point?
quiz.a: V<sub>l</sub> is not negligible, the vapour is not ideal, and ΔH varies.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial vapour-pressure data are often fitted with the Antoine equation, log₁₀ P = A − B/(T + C), a practical cousin of this equation, and simulators use Wagner or DIPPR correlations near the critical point. The same slope argument gives the pressure needed in a pressure cooker and the boiling point of water on a mountain. Search next for the Antoine equation and the Watson correlation for latent heat.
